https://telex.hu/karakter/kultura/2026/0.text: Menü Kereső Meghalt Kárpáti Tamás újságíró, műgyűjtő Kultúra Fotó: Kovács Attila / Collegium Hungaricum Kovács Pál 80 éves korában meghalt Kárpáti Tamás újságíró, műgyűjtő, a Magyar Távirati Iroda egykori főmunkatársa – írja a Papageno . Kárpáti Tamás 1946. március 29-én született Budapesten. Gimnázium után elvégezte a MÚOSZ Újságíró Iskoláját, majd 1965 és 1989 között az MTI turnusvezetője és főmunkatársa volt. 1989-től szabadúszóként dolgozott, volt az Elite magazin főszerkesztője, 2000-ben pedig létrehozta a Premier című művészeti magazint. Rendszeresen írt az Élet és Irodalomba. Főként művészetről és a sportról írt világát ölelték fel, de rendszeresen publikált az Élet és Irodalom hasábjain is, több könyvet írt. Műgyűjtőként kortárs magyar képzőművészek alkotásait gyűjtötte az 1980-as évektől kezdődően. A Hungarikonok című gyűjteménye magyar művészek, sportolók és feltalálók személyes tárgyait tartalmazza, már több mint 150 darabot foglal magába – például John Lennon nyakkendőjét, és egy ecsetet is Frida Kahlotól. A gyűjtemény a Hazatért Hungarikonok című köteteiben is megtekinthető. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

(KY3) - While some communities are taking down license plate reading cameras, one community is considering installing them. Warsaw Police used a grant to buy six license plate reader cameras. But where they will go, or if they will go up at all, is being ironed out. The Warsaw Board of Aldermen put together a special meeting ahead of their regularly scheduled meeting Wednesday night to discuss license plate reader cameras in the city. Warsaw’s police department applied for a grant in 2025 to purchase six. “We started this back in the fall of 2025, applying for the grant, getting the grant, doing a bunch of quotes, signing up with MOUs with the Highway Patrol and working on other ones to where we can mount the cameras and get them put in place,” said Warsaw’s Police Chief, Jason Wenberg. That grant allowed the Warsaw Police Department to purchase six Verkada license plate readers. “We’ve had cars that get stolen,” said Chief Wenberg. “We are a retirement community, so we have a lot of, we possibly could have a lot of silver alerts. And then your amber alerts, and we have a lot of lake traffic rolling through during our tourist time.” Chief Wenberg says the department ultimately decided to go with Verkada license plate readers over other options, like Flock cameras, because of its closed network. “So our system does not do the network sharing, which is the big scrutiny: the network sharing. No other agency will have access to it; it’s only Warsaw’s data,” said Chief Wenberg. Still, some who live in Warsaw have questions and went to a special board of aldermen meeting hoping to get some answers. “We just decided that maybe a public hearing would be best moving forward to get community input and see what everybody’s thoughts were before we decided fully what we were going to do moving forward,” said Warsaw Alderman Kaci Cooner. The Warsaw Police Department has six cameras in their possession that they ordered back in 2025, but they still need to jump through a few hoops before they can actually go into the ground. “In our next meeting, we will have a major discussion about whether we are choosing to move forward with putting them up at all, what the locations will be,” said Cooner. Warsaw’s next Board of Aldermen meeting is scheduled for Wednesday, September 16. To report a correction or typo, please email digitalnews@ky3.com . https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/15/hungary-.text: Hungary, in central Europe, has played a major part in the movie business since the late 19th century. Movies including "Dune," "Evita," "Inferno" and the forthcoming "Wicker" film were shot in Budapest and other parts of Hungary. Hungary's government said it aimed to provide a "stable and predictable framework" for film-making after the former administration capped a key incentive last year. Think of Academy Award-winning movies such as "Poor Things," "Blade Runner 2049" and "The Brutalist" and you might assume they were made in Los Angeles. But instead of being produced in California's famous studios, they were all shot largely in one central European country: Hungary. Huge production complexes, a variety of land and cityscapes and generous incentives have made Hungary a hub for Hollywood. Arnold Schwarzenegger, Tom Cruise, Eddie Redmayne, Liam Hemsworth, Anne Hathaway and Dakota Fanning were all reportedly seen in Hungary's capital Budapest and its surrounding areas this year. Hungary's history of movie-making Hungary has been involved with cinema since its earliest days. The Lumière brothers, makers of the cinematograph device, brought their invention to Budapest's Grand Hotel Royal in 1896 — just months after its Paris debut — and had camera operators film landmarks in the city the same year. When Budapest's artists and writers saw the early movies they "lost their minds in a good way, and almost immediately started creating their own films," according to movie director Justin Reardon, who runs production firm The Royal Budapest Film Company with his wife Barbara. The first Hungarian film staged for the screen was shot in 1901 on the rooftop of the Uránia , a Budapest palace that hosted science presentations, which is now a "cathedral"-like movie theater, he said. Hungarians have also had an outsized influence on the American movie industry. Adolph Zukor, born in the then Austro-Hungarian empire, emigrated at 16 to the U.S., and in 1912 co-founded Paramount Pictures, while William Fox — born Vilmos Fried — was the Hungarian-American founder of the Fox Film Corporation that became Twentieth Century-Fox in 1935. Actors Zsa Zsa Gabor, Tony Curtis, Rachel Weisz and Adrien Brody have Hungarian roots, while Budapest-born Gábor Csupó founded a Hollywood studio that produced early seasons of "The Simpsons." 'Different looks' With its grand architecture as well as areas that appear a little more gritty, Budapest has doubled for European cities such as Paris, Berlin and Rome in movies including "Evita," "Max," and "Inferno." "It's got many different looks," said producer Barbara Reardon. It's also easy to get around, and international movie executives feel at home, she said. "Budapest is equipped with a little bit of everything. You can find your green juices and healthy salads ... and a lot of studio heads and and actors, they like that," she told CNBC by video call. For author Judy Laufer, Budapest as a movie location has a personal connection: her family escaped from the city during the 1956 Hungarian Revolution, fleeing across the border to Austria before emigrating to Canada. Laufer is the producer of an independent movie, "Ashes to Iron," which tells her family's story and was shot in Hungary. "Unless there's a specific thing that tells you you're in Budapest, like the big synagogue, for instance ... you really could be anywhere," Laufer said, referring to a large synagogue on Dohány Street, the thoroughfare where she lived for the first year-and-a-half of her life. Laufer is submitting the movie to film festivals including Sundance and Berlin and will hold a private screening in Budapest to mark the 70-year anniversary of the revolution later this month. Other locations for "Ashes to Iron" include a small airport and a nature trail outside Budapest. Barbara Reardon said the country is also attractive for filming because of the proximity to multiple different types of landscapes. "Outside of the city, you have the lake that you can double for a sea," she said, referring to Lake Balaton , central Europe's largest freshwater lake. "Maybe we don't have mountains, but nowadays that's an easy fix, [as] the surrounding countries do." 'Stable' incentives While the Hungarian studios can't compete in size with California's Warner Bros. Studios Burbank or Universal Studios, they can compete on price. Production costs are around 30% to 50% cheaper than in the U.S., according to Barbara Reardon. About a 20-minute drive north of Budapest is Origo Studios, a complex where large chunks of U.S. movies including "Dune," "Dune: Part Two" and "Inferno" were shot. The studio has 11 stages plus 4 acres of backlot (where movie sets for outdoor scenes are built) and was founded in 2010 in a partnership with U.S. production company Raleigh Studios, run by American studio executive Michael Moore at the time. When CNBC visited Origo Studios in August, it was quiet. CEO Márta Fekszi Horváth described it as a "transition period," but added that she was "very optimistic" about forthcoming productions. Hungary's movie industry was thrown into disarray after former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán paused an incentive scheme that provided a 30% rebate on all production spend in the country. While the scheme was restarted in December, the former government also put a cap on the value of productions for the first half of 2026, adding to the uncertainty as producers tend to plan budgets a year ahead or more. The new government has submitted proposals to supplement the rebate by 63 billion Hungarian forints ($193 million), Horváth said, and last month, Hungary's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Anita Orbán sought to reassure the movie industry further, saying that the new administration aimed to provide a "stable and predictable framework" for the incentive system. The government wanted to bring "even more" international productions to the country, she added. Local talent One large-scale production that was shot in Hungary and is set for release in the U.S. and U.K. this month is "Wicker," starring Olivia Colman as an ostracized, single fisherwoman and Alexander Skarsgård as her custom-ordered husband crafted out of willow. It was filmed on two medieval backlots at Korda Studios and the National Film Institute, to the west and north of the city respectively, according to Barbara Reardon, a local co-producer. Hollywood studios often want to bring in their own teams to oversee certain functions, or may take post-production back home, according to the Reardons. But Barbara said she's seen a shift. "'Wicker' ... was one of the first big international films with big international stars that hired [a] local production designer, local costume designer, local hair and makeup designer," she said. The movie's writer-directors, Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer, set the film "outside of a specific time and place, which meant we got to invent our own culture," Fischer said in production notes seen by CNBC. The movie's costume designers, András Dániel Tóth and Attila Godena-Juhász, who are Hungarian, were inspired by Hungary's traditional clothing, such as bridal headpieces with layered veils, and Wilson said the country's folk art and traditions shaped how "Wicker" looks. For a "tiny little" country, Hungary punches above its weight, Justin Reardon said. "You don't expect in a very small market to have such a robust group of people that are able to to accomplish so much." https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/hungarian-pr.text: Europe Hungarian premier says Budapest, Kyiv agree to build ‘new foundation’ for political, economic ties Peter Magyar holds 1st meeting with Ukrainian president amid EU leaders’ summit in Brussels, expresses ‘full solidarity’ with Kyiv amid Russia-Ukraine war Burc Eruygur 17 October 2026 • Update : 17 October 2026 ISTANBUL Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said Friday that Budapest and Kyiv agreed to build a “new foundation” for their political and economic ties. Magyar announced the agreement in a statement on US social media company X after a first meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Brussels, where they attended an EU leaders’ summit. Welcoming Hungary and Ukraine’s agreement to strengthen the rights of the Hungarian minority in the Zakarpattia region, Magyar said Budapest sees the Ukrainian parliament’s adoption and implementation of a minority education law as a “first step towards rebuilding mutual trust.” “I thanked the Ukrainian Parliament for its September resolution recognizing the crimes committed against Hungarians in Transcarpathia through forced labor and mass deportations between 1944 and 1946,” said Magyar further. He went on to say that he and Zelenskyy agreed to continue ministerial-level talks, focusing particularly on improving the situation of minorities in both countries. “We also agreed that it is in both countries’ interests to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations,” said Magyar, going on to express full solidarity with Kyiv amid the ongoing war. “Hungary is ready to use every possible diplomatic means to help achieve a ceasefire as soon as possible and secure lasting peace,” Magyar added. Zelenskyy said he and the Hungarian prime minister discussed key agenda items and Ukraine's progress toward EU accession, thanking Magyar for his “principled steps” and for opening two more EU negotiating clusters. “We are working to open the remaining two by the end of the year,” said Zelenskyy, noting they discussed the diplomatic situation and efforts to end the over-four-year war. Zelenskyy said they also discussed opportunities for cooperation between Ukraine and Hungary, as well as trade and issues related to agricultural products. “Ukraine always stands for good-neighborly relations and mutual strengthening. We agreed to resume joint work at various levels and to exchange visits. Our teams will work out the dates,” Zelenskyy added. Following the meeting, Budapest and Kyiv’s top diplomats also held talks in Brussels, during which Andrii Sybiha congratulated her Hungarian counterpart “on the new chapter in our relations.” “We witness a full reset in political, economic, humanitarian, and other areas. We still have a lot on our agenda, and work continues on many important issues. But we can already say it clearly: this is a new chapter. It’s history. Together, we have proven that quiet diplomacy pays off. It is always better to focus on concrete results and deliver them,” Sybiha added. The meeting follows years of friction between Ukraine and Hungary, when Hungary possessed close ties with Russia under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription contact_the_ombudsman is_there_an_error_in_this_story ombudsman_apply_button LATEST NEWS All Polish president meets Supreme Court chief amid Constitutional Tribunal standoff Polish opposition party calls for protest outside Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw Russian foreign minister says he had 'not bad, though brief' talks with Rubio on G20 sidelines Polymarket probing suspicious bets on Israeli election: Report Oman evacuates injured crew from Indian boat targeted in Strait of Hormuz Iran says 4th oil tanker hit mine, caught fire in Strait of Hormuz Top US diplomat urges G20 members to focus on economic cooperation See All UK premier offers Scotland more regional powers, urges cooperation Poland plans to let railway guards neutralize drones amid sabotage fears

https://aa.com.tr/en/europe/polish-presi.text: Europe Polish president meets Supreme Court chief amid Constitutional Tribunal standoff US ambassador describes situation as ‘very serious,’ says 2 sides presenting ‘diametrically different versions’ of events Jo Harper 31 October 2026 • Update : 31 October 2026 WARSAW Polish President Karol Nawrocki returned to Warsaw late Friday after cutting short a trip to Senegal and met Supreme Court First President Zbigniew Kapinski amid an escalating standoff over control of the Constitutional Tribunal. Nawrocki landed shortly before 10 pm local time (2100GMT) after turning his plane around above Spain, saying the president had to be in Poland because of events at the court. Kapinski earlier condemned the events at the tribunal and said disputes over constitutional institutions could not justify actions that paralyzed them or stripped them of authority. He said the constitution and law set the limits of state power, “not political decisions or demonstrations of force.” The confrontation remained tense late Friday as opposition politicians and demonstrators gathered outside the tribunal. Law and Justice (PiS) leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski accused the government of preparing to use force against opponents and urged them to “win the battle for Poland.” Piotr Duda, head of the Solidarity trade union, also sharply escalated the rhetoric, addressing Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski and Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek. “Do you want a war? Then you shall have one,” he said, calling on Solidarity members to gather outside the tribunal. US Ambassador Tom Rose described the situation as “very serious” and said the two sides were presenting “diametrically different versions” of events. “We may be witnessing an unprecedented confrontation concerning the government’s use of state power and the independence and authority of a constitutional institution,” Rose said. He urged state officials, police and demonstrators to avoid actions that could provoke violence or further escalation, adding that Washington would not judge or interfere in Poland’s internal dispute. The crisis also drew comment from Moscow, with Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova mocking Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski over the confrontation. Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who said she had assumed control of the tribunal, indicated late Friday that Nawrocki could come to the court for talks, but only without accompanying officials. She said conditions had been prepared for a meeting with the president, while rejecting the possibility of other officials entering with him because of security concerns. Police remained deployed around the tribunal but said officers had not entered the building. The standoff began after orders appeared to suspend Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice President Bartlomiej Sochanski.
